title: Course introduction
lead: Database systems: motivation, definitions, data abstraction and the scope of the Edinburgh course.
goals: Abstraction, data models and course scope

sections.title: Motivation for database systems
sections.html:
Database systems store and process the data used by applications. The course studies the principles that allow this processing to remain efficient as data volume and the number of users grow. These principles include data independence, declarative queries, concurrency and reliable storage.

The introductory slides motivate this subject through application data, scientific data and the difference between data growth and processing capacity. Their numerical charts describe the sources and dates shown in the slides; they are background context, rather than parameters used by the later algorithms.

PDF pp. 1–9

sections.title: Database, DBMS and file-based storage
sections.html:
A database is an organised collection of related data representing a domain. A database management system (DBMS) is the software that stores, manages and provides access to that collection. The course mainly concerns relational DBMSs.

The slides use a university database with Instructor and Course relations. Storing these relations in CSV files requires application code to parse records, search for values and coordinate changes. Repeated facts create redundancy; application code becomes dependent on the file format.

A DBMS centralises query execution, integrity constraints, atomic updates, concurrent access, permissions and programmatic access. Atomicity prevents a failed operation from leaving only part of a required update. Concurrency control coordinates operations from different users. These are separate system responsibilities.

PDF pp. 10–17

sections.title: Abstraction, data models and course scope
sections.html:
The physical level describes the representation of records in storage. The logical level describes the data and its structure. The view level exposes selected information to an application or user. Data independence limits the effect of changes at lower levels on higher levels.

A data model supplies the concepts used to describe data. A schema describes a particular database using that model; an instance is the current data satisfying the schema. Relational, key-value, document and graph models provide different concepts.

The technical sequence covers disk-oriented storage, indexes, query evaluation and optimisation, transactions, and distributed and parallel databases. Query theory supplies precise definitions and complexity results. The assumed background includes introductory databases, algorithm analysis and programming.

PDF pp. 18–24

sections.title: Edinburgh course organisation and references
sections.html:
The remaining introductory slides describe the Edinburgh Spring 2026 teaching team, lectures, revision classes, assessment, textbooks and communication channels. The lecture sequence has three blocks: database/query-language revision, DBMS internals and query-evaluation theory.

Ramakrishnan and Gehrke is the main systems reference; the linked database-theory text supports the theory block. The source also states Edinburgh-specific assignment and examination rules. Consult the source for those historical arrangements; they do not establish deadlines or assessment requirements for another university.

PDF pp. 25–36

quiz.question: Changing a record’s byte position primarily belongs to which level?
quiz.explanation: A byte position is a physical representation detail; the schema describes the meaning and structure of the data.
